episodes.212242: Multiple thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening of the May 27th across central and southwest Virginia as a strong upper level disturbance passed across the lower Mid-Atlantic along a stationary front draped across the region. The storms developed in a moderately unstable environment, with surface temperatures observed in the low to mid 80s during the afternoon, while dewpoints were observed in the upper 60s to low 70s. This helped to drive MLCAPE values into the 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg range, with relatively steep low-level lapse rates. Area wind profilers also indicated westerly winds within the low levels of the atmosphere, with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear supporting damaging wind gusts in the stronger thunderstorm activity.

episodes.212253: On the 27th afternoon, slow-moving thunderstorms produced heavy to locally extreme rainfall, including a public observation of 3.14 inches in the Wichita Hill neighborhood of  far southwestern Marion County.  Flash flooding was limited to adjacent far northeastern Morgan County, focused along Mann Road.

episodes.212616: Difluence ahead of an incoming shortwave interacted with ample moisture across west Texas and southeast New Mexico, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop across the area during the morning of the 26th. The biggest issue during the morning was training thunderstorms which, combined with heavy rainfall, yielded flash flooding for numerous locations. Later that evening, storms redeveloped in southeast New Mexico and moved into portions of west Texas. Large hail and strong winds were observed with these storms.

episodes.212893: A mainly stationary front sprawled across southeast Ohio and West Virginia on the 26th and 27th of May, then a cold front arrived and sank down through the middle Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. This second front exited to the south by mid day on the 28th.  Precipitation spread north across the area on the 26th, then additional rounds of rain and storms continued to traverse the area through the 27th. ||Soils were already saturated from previous rainfall, then an additional one to three inches of rain fell over the area. One strip of three to four inches fell over portions of Gilmer, Lewis, and Barbour counties. This excessive rainfall prompted minor flooding on portions of the Little Kanawha and West Fork Rivers as well as flooded roads in Barbour, Gilmer, Harrison, Jackson, Lewis, Mason, Roane, and Randolph Counties. Mud and rock slides also occurred in Harrison and Wirt Counties.  Strong to severe thunderstorms in the afternoon of the 27th produced wind damage that download trees and power lines in Boone, Harrison, Mason, Jackson, Lewis, Roane, and Upshur Counties.
episodes.212903: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.

episodes.213034: Weak upper ridging persisted across the forecast area on 5/26, but seasonable instability, PWAT's near 2, and enhanced moisture convergence led to scattered thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening hours. One isolated severe storm in Aiken County produced tree damage before training, slow moving convection produced two instances of flash flooding in Orangeburg County.
episodes.213065: Deep moisture pooled across the lower Mid-Atlantic during the afternoon and evening of the 26th to the south of a stationary front draped across northern Virginia. Precipitable water values were estimated in the 1.8 to 1.9 inch range across the New River Valley area of Virginia per Storm Prediction Center Meso-analysis, while CAPE values were estimated to range from 1,500 to 2,000 J/kg during the evening. A series of thunderstorms were observed training across the southern half of Pulaski County, VA beginning around 6 PM EDT, with cells passing from west to east across the area through 9 PM EDT. Multiple cells were estimated by radar to have produced rainfall rates of 3 to 4 inches per hour. Dry antecedent conditions were noted for all of Pulaski County, with D2: Severe Drought highlighted by the U.S. Drought Monitor.  It was estimated that between 4 and 6 inches or rain fell within the headwaters of Big Macks Creek.  MRMS FLASH did not present impressive returns, and was offset from the Big Macks Creek basin by 3-5 miles to the west. FLASH estimated the rainfall reached into the 50 to 70-year Average Recurrence Interval range for a 6-hour duration along a narrow north to south strip west of the basin, with rainfall totals reaching 180 percent of the 6-hour Flash Flood Guidance. CREST Unit Streamflow ranged from 125 to 250 cfs per mi^2 during the event.
episodes.213207: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across North and Central Texas on May 27 and 28, triggered by a slow-moving upper-level disturbance. Although the majority of these storms remained sub-severe, a few produced large hail. Additionally, the slow progression of the system led to heavy rainfall and flash flooding in some areas.
episodes.213210: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on a daily basis across the region over Memorial Day weekend as a result of several passing upper level disturbances. Some storms produced severe hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Significant flash flooding occurred in North Richland Hills in Tarrant County on May 25th.
episodes.213383: In a warm southwest flow regime ahead of a weak cold front, a very moist air mass combined with moderate instability and improved shear resulted in a couple of organized lines of storms with damaging winds. One moved across the far northeastern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain, including Warren and Halifax counties, while the other affected Chatham, Moore, and Lee counties. There were numerous reports of downed trees and power lines in these areas.
episodes.213386: Showers and thunderstorms fired along a stalled frontal boundary throughout the day, resulting in localized heavy rainfall and flooding.
episodes.213568: Thunderstorms increased across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 27th, as an upper level low pressure system approached the region. The air mass became moderately unstable during the afternoon, and wind shear northeast of the surface low pressure center across southeastern Oklahoma became supportive of rotating storms. Two tornadoes developed from these thunderstorms.
episodes.213629: Showers and thunderstorms developed along an east-west oriented stationary boundary draped across northern West Virginia in the afternoon and evening hours. 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported storm organization reaching severe levels, and the strongest storms produced wind damage with reports of trees down within the strongest storms.
episodes.213648: Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the Gulf waters and bays.
episodes.213650: Isolated thunderstorm damage occurred over northern Harris county.
episodes.213666: An upper-level trough brought in enough moisture and instability to produce isolated severe thunderstorms over Central MT. Dry air at the surface helped storms produce severe wind gusts.
episodes.213777: During the evening hours on May 26th, a couple strong to severe storms produced penny to quarter sized hail in portions of Mower County.
episodes.213778: During the late afternoon and evening hours on May 27th, a cluster of strong to severe storms produced up to quarter sized hail across portions of Clark and Jackson counties. Additionally, some instances of tree damage due to straight-line winds were noted in Adams County.

Other storms formed east of the dryline in a conditionally unstable, moist airmass. Storms produced all severe hazards and locally heavy rain.
episodes.214087: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across western North Carolina during the afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in the Piedmont, while an isolated flash flood event occurred in Caldwell County.
episodes.214089: Another round of scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across the South Carolina Piedmont during the afternoon and evening. Weak winds and a weakly convergence boundary in the presence of marginal moisture led to the development of high-based convection, which featured a widely viewed landspout that drifted west-southwest from Minnesota into South Dakota.
episodes.214426: Locally induced afternoon thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall over Aguada, causing minor flooding on May 27th.
episodes.214428: During the morning hours of May 27th, a squall line of strong to severe thunderstorms associated with a Mesoscale Convective System and outflow boundary from thunderstorms further upstream, resulted in numerous thunderstorm wind gusts, as well as welcome rainfall but no significant flooding.  Some of the gusts reached severe limits in the lower Rio Grande Valley (Cameron).
episodes.214429: During the morning hours of May 27th, a squall line of severe thunderstorms associated with a Mesoscale Convective System and outflow boundary from thunderstorms further upstream, resulted in numerous thunderstorm wind gusts by late morning as it reached the Laguna Madre and the nearshore Gulf waters, adjacent to the Lower Texas coast.  Gale to Storm-Force winds were common along the line.

A total of 4 to 6 inches of rain fell within the headwaters of Big Macks Creek.  Of this total,  3 to 5 inches of rain fell in 1.5 hours.  Max Creek Road was impassible, with 2 of the 7 bridges leading into Camp Powhatan sustaining damage. The estimated water depth in Big Macks Creek was 9 feet higher than base flow.  Debris was observed having been washed onto some of the bridges.  Runoff caused Lake Powhatan to rise 3 to 4 feet.

Other reportes of flooded roads were received via Social Media from the Ora and Waterloo areas.

A National Weather Service storm survey team conducted a damage survey of areas in Kirby. The team concluded that severe downdraft winds, associated with a supercell thunderstorm, impacted the community of Kirby resulting in sporadic damage. Imagery and drone footage from the Texas Department of Emergency Management (TDEM) and the Bexar County Office of Emergency Management, in addition to the NWS ground survey, noted intermittent damage to trees and fences, mainly south of Binz Engleman Rd. Damage included medium to large tree branches snapped, several downed fences and a few locations with sheet metal damage on structures. The most concentrated area of damage was located near James Webb Dr. where a carport roof was displaced. The visible damage is indicative of maximum wind speeds of approximately 75 mph.

A landspout formed around 2 miles northwest of Hills, southwest of the intersection of 40th Avenue and 51st Street.  The highly visible tornado was viewed from numerous angles as it traversed slowly across open fields to the west-southwest.  The tornado crossed the state line out of Rock County one-half mile south of 41st Street on 488th Avenue. The landspout continued west-southwest through Minnehaha County for less than one mile before it dissipated at 1626CST. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating in either Rock County or Minnehaha County, giving the tornado a rating of EFU in both counties. The average path width was estimated at 40 yards based on video and photo evidence.
